newsitem.title: USA: Inventory bulge seen slowing US Q4 industry output.
newsitem.headline: Inventory bulge seen slowing US Q4 industry output.

text.p: The U.S. manufacturing sector will likely soften in the fourth quarter as some inventory overhang at the retail level may keep industries from increasing output, Wall Street analysts said.
Higher retail inventory "is going to act as a constraint on production in the fourth quarter," said Robert Dederick, chief economist at Northern Trust Co.

The retail inventory accumulation carried over from the third quarter is expected to keep industrial production slow even if consumers decide to return to the stores with gusto for year-end holiday shopping, pundits said.

"I guess we're now in the process of liquidating (the inventory build-up) and that's why industrial production is so soft," said William Griggs, managing director at consulting firm Griggs & Santow Inc.
A slew of economic reports released on Friday showed that business inventories were up 0.1 percent in September, against a revised 0.3 percent in August.
Analysts said the small increase was due to a drop in wholesale inventories, which fell 1.28 percent.
A breakdown of the number, however, showed manufacturers' inventories were up 0.3 percent in September versus August, while retailers' holdings jumped 0.84 percent in the period.
Automobile inventory was up a brisk 1.4 percent in the period as major manufacturers increased production on fears of a major strike by U.S. auto workers.
Analysts estimate the economy now has around $2.0 to $3.0 billion in inventories to liquidate at the manufacturing level and about $6.0 to $7.0 billion to burn at the retail level.

"In the wholesale sector you probably don't have much at all to liquidate," said an analyst at a U.S. bank who asked not to be named. "Most of the problem is in the manufacturing and the retail sectors," he added.
Industrial production and capacity utilization data released by the Federal Reserve on Friday confirmed Wall Street's forecast of faltering industrial production.
October output was down 0.5 percent against a 0.3 percent rise in the previous month. Capacity utilization slipped to 82.7 percent against 83.4 percent earlier.

Analysts said the report showed a weak reading even though a decline in auto production -- due mostly to a strike at General Motors in Canada, which forced some plants to shut in the U.S. -- was responsible for most of the drop.
"Ex-auto the number still would've been down 0.1 percent," said Elliott Platt, director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette.
"The numbers suggest businesses probably are ... cutting back production in order to make sure there's no excess build-up in inventory," Platt added.
Most analysts said, however, they were not extremely concerned about an inventory overhang problem going into the next year.

They said they expect consumer spending to pick up in the fourth quarter from the very low levels registered in the third quarter, which may, as a result, clear part of the inventory buildup and prop up some production in the pipeline.

"I'd think we're going to be pretty much living out of inventory, production will be on the sluggish side but I think final sales will come back and you're not going to go into next year with a big problem," Griggs said.
